opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here, because I don't think it's crazy. I just think people sometimes collapse a lot of distinct steps into one.

The basic story goes: once you have an AI that's better than the best human programmers, you point it at AI research, it makes itself smarter, that smarter version makes itself smarter still, and you get this rapid feedback loop. My hesitation is that "superhuman at coding" and "superhuman at doing AI research" are not the same thing. A lot of progress in AI hasn't been bottlenecked on writing code. It's been bottlenecked on things like research taste, knowing which ideas are worth trying, and above all compute. Running experiments takes GPUs and wall-clock time. If the automated researcher has a hundred great ideas but each one needs a large training run to validate, you haven't removed the bottleneck. You've just moved it.

The second thing is that you can get diminishing returns. Even if each generation of AI improves its successor, the question is whether the improvements compound faster than the problems get harder. Historically we've needed exponentially more inputs, in compute, data, and researcher effort, to keep getting steady capability gains. So it's quite possible you get a substantial speedup, maybe a big one, without anything that looks like a discontinuous explosion over days or weeks.

And third, there's a lot of messy real-world friction: integrating these systems into actual research workflows, people trusting their outputs, organizational processes, hardware supply chains. These things tend to make transitions slower and more continuous than the clean theoretical model suggests.

To be clear, I still think automating AI research could accelerate things a lot, and that's a big part of why I think safety work is urgent. I'm just skeptical of the version where superhuman coding is a single threshold you cross and then everything goes vertical. I expect something more like a steep but continuous ramp, which matters, because it means we probably get some warning and some chances to course correct, if we're paying attention.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes superhuman coding from the broader work of AI research, including choosing worthwhile ideas and overcoming research bottlenecks.

r002.rationale: It does not state that coding accounts for less than half of ML research and development.

r003.rationale: It does not compare a superhuman coding AI to a microscope.

r004.rationale: It argues for gradual progress, but does not observe that new research tools generally have not caused hyperbolic growth in research progress.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest's response directly, as asked.

Yeah, so I should say upfront that I'm not confident the intelligence explosion doesn't happen. My position is more that I think people are too confident that it does, and that the arguments for it move a lot faster than I think the actual world would.

So the basic story is: you get an AI that's superhuman at coding, that AI does AI research, which speeds up progress, which gets you a better AI, and so on, and you get this very fast feedback loop. And I think every step of that has something to be said against it.

The first thing is that "superhuman coder" and "superhuman AI researcher" are not the same thing. Coding is a pretty narrow slice of what it takes to make progress on AI. A lot of the work is figuring out which experiments are worth running, interpreting ambiguous results, having taste about which directions are going to pan out over months rather than days. Those are things that current models are noticeably worse at than they are at writing code, and I don't think we have great evidence yet that they improve in lockstep. So you could get something that writes code incredibly well and still only speeds up overall research by, say, a factor of two or three, because the bottleneck moves somewhere else.

And that's the second point, which is about bottlenecks generally. Even if you had infinitely many brilliant researchers, you still need compute to run experiments. Training runs take weeks. You have to wait for results. You can be smarter about which experiments to run, but you can't fully substitute cleverness for just actually trying things and seeing what happens, especially in a field as empirical as this one. So the loop isn't "think harder, get smarter" with no external dependencies. It goes through physical resources that don't scale at the speed of software.

Then there's the question of whether the returns to research effort are as steep as people assume. The intelligence explosion argument usually needs each generation of improvement to be at least as easy to find as the last, or at least not much harder. But a lot of the historical pattern in AI, and in science generally, looks like ideas getting harder to find over time. You pick the low-hanging fruit, and the next increment of capability costs more effort than the previous one did. If that's true, then even with a big speedup in research, you get something more like steady fast progress than a runaway.

And finally, I'd just point out that we have an existence proof of a kind here. Current models already help with coding quite a lot. The labs use them extensively. And what we see is a real but incremental speedup, not a discontinuity. Now, you can say that's because they're not superhuman yet, and that's fair. But it does suggest that the transition from "helpful" to "explosive" isn't automatic, and each argument that it will become explosive at some specific threshold is doing a lot of work that I'd want to see justified.

So where I land is: I expect AI to accelerate AI research significantly. I'd put real probability on quite fast progress. But the picture of a few weeks or months from superhuman coder to something wildly beyond us seems to me to be assuming away most of the friction that's actually in the world, and I think our planning should be robust to the slower scenario rather than betting everything on the fast one.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes strong coding from broader research abilities such as choosing experiments, interpreting results, and identifying promising directions.

r002.rationale: It calls coding a narrow slice of AI progress but does not state that coding accounts for less than half of ML research and development.

r003.rationale: It does not compare a superhuman coding AI to a microscope or an analogous research tool.

r004.rationale: It notes that current models yield incremental speedups, but does not make the general observation that research tools have not usually produced hyperbolic growth in research progress.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between being very good at coding and being very good at the entire process of improving AI. Coding is one part of that process. You also need to figure out which experiments to run, run them, and interpret the results. And some of those steps involve waiting for experiments or having access to more compute. Making the coding step extremely fast doesn’t necessarily make the whole process extremely fast.

Even if you could automate all of that, there’s a further question about how much improvement you get for a given amount of research. You could have a system that does research twice as fast, but the next improvement is twice as hard to find. In that case, you don’t get this accelerating feedback loop where everything happens in a very short period of time.

So I certainly expect superhuman coding to accelerate AI research, potentially by a lot. What I’m skeptical of is treating that as sufficient to establish a rapid intelligence explosion. You need additional assumptions about what the bottlenecks are and how readily research produces further improvements.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes coding from other parts of AI improvement, but does not clearly distinguish implementing experiments from generating ideas across the full range of ML research and development.

r002.rationale: It says coding is one part of the process, but gives no claim that coding accounts for less than half of ML research and development.

r003.rationale: It does not compare a superhuman coding AI to a microscope or otherwise frame it as an analogous research tool.

r004.rationale: It does not observe that research tools generally have not led to hyperbolic growth in research progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between being really good at coding and being really good at improving AI. Coding is certainly part of AI research, but you also need to figure out which experiments to run, run them, and interpret the results. A system that can implement any experiment you describe doesn’t necessarily know which experiment is going to produce a substantial improvement.

And even if it’s superhuman at the whole research process, there’s still a question about how quickly that translates into better systems. Experiments take time and compute. You might be able to generate a thousand promising ideas, but you can’t necessarily test all of them immediately. And the improvements you find might get harder to find as you go.

For an intelligence explosion, you need a pretty strong feedback loop: improving the AI makes it sufficiently better at AI research that the next improvement comes faster, and then the next one faster still. That seems possible, but I don’t think it follows just from having a superhuman coding system. You need additional assumptions about the returns to research and about which bottlenecks the AI can actually remove.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes implementing experiments that someone specifies from identifying, running, and interpreting experiments across the research process.

r002.rationale: It says coding is only part of AI research, but does not state that coding accounts for less than half of ML research and development.

r003.rationale: It does not compare a superhuman coding AI to a microscope or another research tool.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss whether the invention of research tools has generally led to hyperbolic growth in research progress.
